title: Key Chooser
context: Grade 4, the chapter's recap. An adult sees a key being picked. What is actually being learnt is how a key is chosen, which the chapter asks for twice and never teaches. The route taken is the one the chapter's own pictographs show: every key on its pages turns its data into whole symbols, or whole symbols and a half, and each number is checked against the key in turn. The opening page's airport data and the closing box's points both find a key that way, and the closing box's three questions about the game are replaced by the questions its points can answer.

writeup.why: Choose a key that turns every number into whole symbols, or whole symbols and a half, without needing too many, then draw the pictograph and ask it what its data can answer.
writeup.look: A data card and a key dial at the left, a checker board that lays each number out in symbols, a symbol count at the top, and question cards, a can do list and word cards along the foot.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Key Chooser' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the symbol count, every symbol the trial key would need across the whole card, a half counted as a half, in ink. Beside it are the rows lit against the rows on the card. The symbol count changes whenever the dial turns, and it is recounted row by row as the checker lays each row out. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The data card stands at the left of the working area, 230 by 330 at 64,212. It lists up to six named numbers, each on a line 48 tall with 6 between, from 220. The key dial sits under it, 230 by 90 at 64,556, and turns through trial keys. The set key control sits at the foot, 230 by 60 at 64,660, and unlocks only when every row lights. The checker board fills the rest, 840 by 440 at 306,212, with up to six rows, each 56 tall with 8 between, from 226. Each row has its name in a cell 110 wide, then its symbols from 426, each 36 wide with 6 between, up to fifteen, and a tag 80 wide at 1060. For each number the checker lays out whole symbols one key's worth at a time, and the number on the card goes down by the key as each one lands. When nothing is left, the row lights. When exactly half the key is left, the checker lays the left half of the symbol last, and the row lights. When anything else is left, the leftover stands loose in the tag in amber, and the row stays unlit. No part of a symbol other than a half is ever offered. A row that needs more than fifteen symbols runs on off the board's right edge, torn off there, with its symbol count written under its name. On the fourth phase the board becomes the finished pictograph. A title strip 600 by 44 and a key box 230 by 44 at 916,212 run along its top, both outlined blanks until filled. The rows move down to start at 266. The data card folds to its heading, and six word cards stand in its place, each 230 by 44 with 6 between. They read data, tally marks, pictograph, symbol, title and key, and each turns over to show what it means. The foot band runs under the board, 840 by 66 at 306,662. It holds the question stack at the left and the tray headed not in this data beside it. At the right stands the can do list of the chapter's three statements, each with a tick box. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number is asked for, with a key for a half beside them. A word pad carries the card's own row names and the words fits, does not fit, too many, most, least, same and not in this data. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and every fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in the rows, is green, except where the rows are named by colour. There each row's symbols wear that row's own colour: red, green, blue, yellow or purple. The key's symbol there is plain grey, which stands for one symbol of any colour and is used for nothing else. Amber is what a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, and so are the numbers in a table and the numbers a side ruler writes. Amber too is what half a symbol stands for, what a key leaves over, and a small round counter for one thing counted. A total of every row is reddish purple, and so is a thing a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share. The row a question asks about is marked by a pale sky blue band laid behind its symbols, never over them. So is the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another. Chrome never borrows one of those, and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every table rule, row line, belt, route line, bracket, outlined blank and card edge is near-black, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. Every reading survives with the colour taken away. A fifth mark lies across and not upright, and a half symbol is the left half of the whole. A row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it. No amount is ever drawn as a length of colour: an amount on this stage is symbols, marks, counters or a written number. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. A key is never set while any row is unlit. A card goes to the tray headed not in this data only when nothing on the finished pictograph bears on its question.
writeup.finish: The card shows the data card with the key the child set, every row lit, the pictograph drawn with its title and key, and the question cards answered, with the one the data could not answer set aside.

phases.win: every row lights as whole symbols and the set key control unlocks
phases.does: sets a trial key and watches each number laid out in whole symbols, checking every row
phases.goal: a key that turns every number into whole symbols fits the data
phases.says: Try this key on every number. Does each one come out in whole symbols?
phases.check: Data of twelve, eighteen and thirty. Does a key of six give whole symbols for every number?
phases.feels: the key is laid against every number in turn, and the set key control waits until every row lights
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, give each group a data card and let them try three keys, writing how many symbols each row would need and what each key leaves over. Choosing a key is asked twice in the chapter and taught nowhere. So take the route the chapter's own pictographs show: every key on its pages turns its data into whole symbols, or whole symbols and a half. Check a key against every number in turn, not only the largest. The opening page's airports have around fifteen hundred, nine hundred, six hundred, five hundred and four hundred flights a day. A key of one hundred gives fifteen, nine, six, five and four symbols. Call each airport by its city.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does the key leave over from this number? Second rung, the phase's: has every number been checked? Third rung: the card is cut to two numbers, and the child tries the key on both. The number keys and the dial stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the largest number feels like the hardest to fit, so if it fits the rest seem sure to.
wrong.move: tries a key of three hundred on the first and largest number, sees fifteen hundred make five whole symbols, and sets it.
wrong.screen: the checker lays out every row, not only the first. Fifteen hundred, nine hundred and six hundred light. Five hundred stands at one symbol with two hundred loose in its tag, and four hundred at one with one hundred loose, and both stay unlit. The set key control stays locked.

wrong.why: a key equal to the smallest number makes the shortest row exactly one symbol, which looks tidy.
wrong.move: chooses the smallest number in the data as the key, one hundred and fifty points, so that player gets one symbol.
wrong.screen: the checker lays out every row. Three hundred and one hundred and fifty light. The two rows of two hundred leave fifty loose, two hundred and fifty leaves one hundred, and three hundred and fifty leaves fifty. Half of one hundred and fifty is seventy-five, so all four stay unlit.

phases.screen: a data card of four numbers, the key dial set to a trial key, and the checker board empty
phases.soWhat: A key that turns every number into whole symbols fits the data. Check every number, not only the first.
phases.concept: A key that fits the data

phases.win: the leftover folds into a half symbol and the row lights, and a leftover that is not a half stays loose
phases.does: compares what is left over with half the key, and closes the row with a half symbol when they match
phases.goal: a key may leave a half symbol, when exactly half the key is left over
phases.says: What is left over? Is it exactly half of the key?
phases.check: With a key of four, how many symbols show twenty-two?
phases.feels: what is left over is laid against half the key, and either it matches or it stays loose
phases.hands: Take the opening page's airports again with a key of two hundred. Nine hundred is four symbols and one hundred over, and one hundred is exactly half the key, so that row ends in a half. Every row fits that way, so two hundred fits as well as one hundred. Then try five hundred, where nine hundred leaves four hundred over, which is not half of five hundred. The chapter draws a half as the left half of the whole, and it draws no other part of a symbol.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is left over? Second rung, the phase's: is that exactly half of the key? Third rung: the card is cut to one number with a small leftover, and the child lays it against the folded symbol. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: a leftover smaller than the key looks too small to draw.
wrong.move: drops the five left over from thirty-five and draws three symbols for a key of ten.
wrong.screen: the checker lays three tens and stands the five at the row's end. The five is laid against the key's symbol folded down its middle, and the two match. A half symbol closes the row, which lights, and the running count shows three and a half. The child's three stays in the slot.

wrong.why: a half was right a moment ago, and it is the only part of a symbol there is.
wrong.move: draws a half for any leftover, so eighty with a key of thirty ends in a half.
wrong.screen: a half symbol is laid at the end of eighty's row, and the checker writes what it stands for, fifteen, beside the loose twenty. The two do not match, so the half comes back off and the twenty stays loose. The row stays unlit.

wrong.why: the first phase lit rows of whole symbols, and a half looks like the key failing.
wrong.move: turns down a key that leaves exactly half over, sure that a key that fits gives whole symbols only.
wrong.screen: the leftover is laid against the folded symbol, and the two match. The half closes the row and the row lights. With every row lit, the set key control unlocks, and the child's choice stays on the dial.

phases.screen: a data card where one number leaves something over, with the checker holding it at the row's end
phases.soWhat: A key may leave a half symbol, when what is left over is exactly half the key.

phases.win: the rows shrink back inside the board and the symbol count drops to a number worth drawing
phases.does: reads the symbol count, then turns the dial to a larger key that still fits every number
phases.goal: too small a key gives too many symbols to draw, even when it fits
phases.says: It fits, but how many symbols is that? Try a bigger key.
phases.check: Data of four hundred and six hundred. Which key fits and is quick to draw, ten or one hundred?
phases.feels: the rows shrink as the key grows, and the count of symbols falls to something a hand could draw
phases.hands: Take the opening page's airports with a key of ten flights. The key fits every number, and the busiest airport alone needs one hundred and fifty symbols. Ask who would draw that. Then try larger keys that still fit. A key of one hundred gives fifteen, nine, six, five and four, and a key of two hundred fits too, with halves. More than one key can fit, so choose one that keeps the rows short enough to draw.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many symbols would this key need? Second rung, the phase's: is there a larger key that still fits? Third rung: the card is cut to two numbers, and the child tries two keys and compares the counts. The number keys and the dial stay open.

wrong.why: a small key gives whole symbols everywhere, and whole symbols have been the aim.
wrong.move: chooses the smallest key that fits, five, for three hundred, five hundred and four hundred and fifty visitors.
wrong.screen: the checker lays out sixty, one hundred and ninety symbols, and every row runs off the board's right edge. The symbol count reads two hundred and fifty. The child's key stays on the dial.

wrong.why: a bigger key gives shorter rows, and shorter rows were the point.
wrong.move: turns straight to a large key, two hundred, and does not check it.
wrong.screen: the checker lays out every row. Three hundred and five hundred each end in a half and light. Four hundred and fifty stands at two symbols with fifty loose, which is not half of two hundred, and stays unlit. The set key control stays locked.

phases.screen: a data card of large numbers with a small trial key, the rows running off the edge of the board
phases.soWhat: Too small a key gives too many symbols. Choose one that fits every number and keeps the rows short.

phases.win: each answer lands on its card, the card the data cannot answer is set aside, and the list is ticked
phases.does: answers each card from the pictograph, sets aside a card the data cannot answer, and ticks the can do list
phases.goal: a finished pictograph answers questions about its own data, and nothing else
phases.says: Can the pictures answer this one? What does the data hold?
phases.check: A pictograph shows books read by four friends. Can it tell who reads fastest?
phases.feels: each card either lights what answers it on the pictograph, or finds nothing there and is set aside
phases.hands: Draw the closing box's points with the class. A key of fifty gives four, five, six, seven, three and four symbols, and a key of one hundred fits as well, with halves. Its three questions ask about the game itself, which the points cannot answer. Do not answer them. Set them aside as not in this data, and ask who scored the most, who the least and which two scored the same. Then tick the can do list against work done, and make the five flashcards and one more for key. The title is the heading that says what a pictograph shows, and the key says what one symbol stands for.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the title say the data is? Second rung, the phase's: does anything on the pictograph bear on this question? Third rung: the stack is cut to two cards, one the data can answer and one it cannot, and the child sorts them. The number keys and the word pad stay open.

wrong.why: the pictograph is about the teams, so a question about a team seems to belong to it.
wrong.move: tries to answer how many players a team has from the pictures.
wrong.screen: the card is laid on the pictograph and nothing on it lights: the title says points, and the key says points. The card slides into the tray headed not in this data, with those words across it.

wrong.why: the most was found by its symbols, and the count came along with it.
wrong.move: gives seven as the most, the number of symbols, when the question asks for points.
wrong.screen: the row is read with the key, seven times twenty-five, and one hundred and seventy-five lands in its tag. The running count shows the seven symbols, and the child's seven stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the pictograph shows each team's points, and a difference is written nowhere on it.
wrong.move: sets aside a card asking how many more points one team scored than another, thinking how many more is not in the data.
wrong.screen: the card is laid on the pictograph, and both rows light. The stretch by which the longer row passes the shorter, four symbols, is banded sky blue and read with the key: one hundred. The card is answered and stays out of the tray.

phases.screen: the finished pictograph with its title and key, a stack of question cards, and the can do list
phases.soWhat: A pictograph answers questions about its own data, such as the most, the least, the same and how many more.

writeup.delight: The third phase, while the dial turns. With each new key every row is laid out afresh in one quick sweep from its left edge. The rows are seen shrinking as the key grows and stretching as it shrinks. A row whose leftover stops fitting lets its loose tag drop from its end, and catches it up again when a key fits it. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the data card stands at the left with four named numbers, the key dial set to a trial key, and the checker board empty. On the second a data card stands where one number leaves something over, with the checker holding it at that row's end. On the third a card of large numbers stands with a small trial key set, and the rows already run off the board's edge. On the fourth the finished pictograph stands with its title and key, the question cards are stacked at its foot, and the can do list waits unticked. The running count at the top left holds the symbol count, with the rows lit beside it, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the key dial, or the leftover at a row's end, or the symbol count, or the top question card, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks its question. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any data set of up to six numbers and any trial key, with the checker, the symbol count, the question cards, the can do list and the word cards all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on keys that fit, keys that leave a half, keys that are too small, and the questions a finished pictograph can and cannot answer.
voiceLines: A card of numbers and a key dial. Which key turns every number into symbols?
Try this key on every number. Does each one come out in whole symbols?
What is left over? Is it exactly half of the key?
It fits, but how many symbols is that? Try a bigger key.
Can the pictures answer this one? What does the data hold?
Another data card. Try the key on every number before you set it.
Free play. Any numbers and any key, with the checker and the cards open.
Check every number again, and read what the key leaves over.
A key checked against every number, the pictograph drawn, and its questions asked.

observations.why: The key went exactly into three numbers and left something other than a half in the other two.
observations.soWhat: A key fits when every number becomes whole symbols, or whole symbols and a half, so check every number.
observations.observe: Three rows lit under a trial key and two stayed unlit, each with a loose leftover in its tag.

observations.why: A half symbol stands for half the key, and the chapter's pictographs draw no other part of a symbol.
observations.soWhat: A key may leave a half. A key that leaves any other part makes a row that whole and half symbols cannot draw.
observations.observe: A leftover of exactly half the key folded into a half symbol, and a leftover of any other size stayed loose.

observations.why: A small key takes many symbols to make each number, and a larger one takes fewer.
observations.soWhat: Too small a key gives too many symbols to draw, even when it fits.
observations.observe: The rows ran off the board under a small key and drew back inside it when the dial turned to a larger key that still fitted.

observations.why: The pictograph holds only the numbers on its card, and that card asked about something else.
observations.soWhat: A finished pictograph answers questions about its own data, and nothing else.
observations.observe: The cards about the most, the least and the same were answered, and one card went to the tray headed not in this data.

serves.exercise: drawing a pictograph of the daily flights at five airports, the instruction the opening page ends on
returning to the opening page's airport data to answer the related question, which points back at its instruction
ticking the self-assessment list of three things you can do
making flashcards for the five vocabulary words and quizzing a partner
choosing a key and drawing a pictograph of the points six players scored in a tournament, with the three questions printed under it

source_tool.description: A data card at the left of the stage lists a set of numbers with their names, and a key dial beside it sets a trial key. For each number a checker lays out whole symbols, one for each key's worth, and shows what is left over. When nothing is left, the row lights as whole symbols. When exactly half the key is left, a half symbol closes the row and it lights. When anything else is left, a loose tag at the row's end gives the number left over, which no symbol can draw, and that row stays unlit. A symbol count at the top left adds every symbol the trial key would need, and a row that runs past the edge of the board is drawn running off it, so a key that is too small is seen to be too small. A key that passes every row can be set, and the pictograph is drawn with a title strip and a key box to fill. Question cards then ask the finished pictograph things: which has the most, which the least, which two are the same, how many more. A card whose question the data cannot answer is set aside with the words not in this data written across it. A can do list of the chapter's three statements, ticked against work on the stage, and six word cards, data, tally marks, pictograph, symbol, title and key, turn over to show a meaning.
source_tool.art_direction: A data card beside a key dial / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a desk with a drawn class and a heap of answer slips, a ruled table, a tally board with a belt of answer cards, pictograph boards with a title strip and a key card, symbols that fold down their middle, a small route map, a tray of picture stamps, and a key dial.
Every pictograph carries a title strip at its top and a key card beside it from the first frame. A title or key still to be filled is an outlined blank, never a space left out.

Every symbol in one pictograph is one plain picture drawn at one size, evenly spaced from the same edge in every row or column, so a row's length is its count of symbols. A face, a kite, a cup, a tree or a bus; no letter, sign or mark ever stands in for a picture.

When the rows of a pictograph name colours, each row's symbols, whole or half, are drawn in that row's colour, and the key's symbol in plain grey. Otherwise every symbol in one pictograph, the key's included, is drawn in one colour.

A half symbol is the left half of the whole symbol, cut down its middle, as the chapter's own keys show it. It always comes last in its row. Halves are the only part of a symbol ever drawn, and only on a key that halves into whole things.
A tally mark is one short upright line. Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, corner to corner, and the next mark starts a new bundle after a small gap.
A pictograph drawn up the page stacks its symbols from the bottom. Its side is left unnumbered, or numbered only in the data's own units, the key times the symbols counted, and never in symbols.

The count of symbols and the number they stand for are never written in the same place: symbols are counted at the top left of the canvas, and a row's number is written at the end of its row with its unit.
The sum of every row is written under the board, labelled as the total for all the rows, and never beside a single row.
A row, a symbol or a mark is told apart by its name or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a tally mark, a symbol, a number, a band or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and the fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that counts in fives cannot afford a bundle whose closing mark has to be hunted for. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in every row, is green, except where the rows are told apart by colour: there every symbol in a row is that row's own colour, red, green, blue, yellow or purple, and the key's symbol is plain grey, a grey used for nothing else, because it stands for a symbol of any colour. What a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, the number written beyond a row's end, the numbers in a table, the numbers a side ruler writes in the data's own units, what half a symbol stands for, and what a key leaves over, is amber. A total of every row, and a thing that a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share, are reddish purple. The row a question asks about, and the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another, are marked by a pale sky blue band behind the symbols or marks. Every table rule, row line, belt, bracket, outlined blank and card border is near-black chrome, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. All of that holds in greyscale, because a fifth mark lies across and not upright, a half symbol is the left half of the whole, a row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Check every number again, and read what the key leaves over.
voice.onNext: Another data card. Try the key on every number before you set it.
voice.opening: A card of numbers and a key dial. Which key turns every number into symbols?
voice.onFinish: A key checked against every number, the pictograph drawn, and its questions asked.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any numbers and any key, with the checker and the cards open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A key that fits the data

placement.where: After groups have tried three keys on a data card, written how many symbols each row would need, and drawn the pictograph with the key they picked, and before the opening page's airport data is drawn. The tool is what checks every number against a key at once, shows what each leaves over, and counts the symbols a key would need, which a pencil does one row at a time.

answer_key.rule: A key fits the data when every number becomes whole symbols, or whole symbols and a half, as the chapter's own pictographs show. To check a key, take each number in turn: if the key goes into it exactly, it is whole symbols; if half the key is left over, the row ends in a half symbol; if anything else is left over, the key does not fit that data. A key can fit and still be too small, needing more symbols than anyone would draw, so choose a key that fits and keeps the rows short enough to draw. A finished pictograph answers questions about its own data, such as the most, the least, the same and how many more, and nothing else.
answer_key.wrong: The checker lays each row out again one key's worth at a time and stands the leftover at the row's end, and the symbol count is recounted as each row is laid, so the child sees which number the key did not fit and how many symbols it would have needed. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Check each number in turn against the key of 15.
30 is 2 fifteens, 45 is 3 fifteens, 60 is 4 fifteens and 15 is 1 fifteen.
Every number gives whole symbols, so the key fits.
items.answer: Yes. It gives 2, 3, 4 and 1 symbols, all whole
items.question: Points scored by four teams are 30, 45, 60 and 15. Would a key of one symbol for 15 points work?
items.checkpoint: A key that turns every number in the data into whole symbols fits.
items.misconception: Checking only the first number, 30, and stopping, when every number must be checked.

steps: 20 is 2 tens, so 2 symbols, and 50 is 5 tens, so 5 symbols.
35 is 3 tens and 5 more, and 5 is half of 10.
So 35 needs 3 whole symbols and a half, and the key still fits.
items.question: The data is 20, 50 and 35, and the key is 10. How many symbols does each number need?
items.checkpoint: A key may leave a half symbol, when what is left over is exactly half the key.
items.misconception: Drawing 35 as 3 symbols and dropping the 5 left over, or as 4 whole symbols.

steps: 300 is 60 fives, 500 is 100 fives and 450 is 90 fives, so the key fits, but that is 250 symbols.
Try a larger key: 300, 500 and 450 are 6, 10 and 9 fifties, all whole.
Too small a key gives too many symbols to draw, even when it fits.
items.answer: No. It needs 60, 100 and 90 symbols, far too many to draw. A key of 50 gives 6, 10 and 9
items.question: A fair counted 300, 500 and 450 visitors on three days. A key of 5 fits every number. Is it a good key?
items.checkpoint: Too small a key gives too many symbols; choose one that fits and keeps the rows short.
items.misconception: Choosing the smallest key that fits because it gives whole symbols, and then drawing a hundred symbols in one row.

steps: Turn each row into points: 7 x 25 = 175, 5 x 25 = 125, 3 x 25 = 75 and 5 x 25 = 125.
Compare: 175 is the most, 75 the fewest, and 125 appears twice, for Teams B and D.
The data counts points only, so it says nothing about players.
items.answer: Team A the most, 175; Team C the fewest, 75; Teams B and D the same, 125 each. It cannot tell how many players a team has
items.question: A pictograph of points scored by four teams, one symbol for 25 points, holds 7 symbols for Team A, 5 for Team B, 3 for Team C and 5 for Team D. Which team scored the most, which the fewest, and which two the same? Can it tell how many players each team has?
items.checkpoint: A pictograph answers questions about its own data, and nothing else.
items.misconception: Trying to answer a question the data does not hold, such as how many players a team has, from the pictures.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: The data is 12, 20 and 8. Does a key of 4 give whole symbols for every number?
The data is 12, 18 and 20. Does a key of 6 give whole symbols for every number?
items.final_answer: No. 12 and 18 give 2 and 3 symbols, but 20 is 3 symbols with 2 left over

items.question: With a key of 4, how many symbols show 18?
items.final_answer: 4 and a half: 16 is 4 symbols, and the 2 left over is half of 4

items.question: The data is 60, 90 and 80. Which key fits, 30 or 20?
items.final_answer: 20. It gives 3, 4 and a half, and 4 symbols. With 30, 80 leaves 20 over, which is neither a whole symbol nor half of 30

items.question: The data is 80, 120 and 40. A key of 2 fits. How many symbols would it need in all, and what is a better key?
items.final_answer: 120 symbols, far too many. A key of 20 gives 4, 6 and 2

items.question: The data is 700, 400 and 900 tickets. Which is the better key, 10 or 100?
items.final_answer: 100. It gives 7, 4 and 9 symbols. A key of 10 fits too, but gives 70, 40 and 90, far too many

items.question: A pictograph of paper boats made by five groups has one boat symbol for 3 boats. It holds 5 symbols for Group A, 8 for B, 2 for C, 5 for D and 7 for E. Which group made the most, which the fewest, and which two made the same number?
items.final_answer: Group B the most, 24; Group C the fewest, 6; Groups A and D the same, 15 each

items.question: Four houses ran laps: Ganga 150, Yamuna 250, Kaveri 100 and Narmada 200. Choose a key that gives whole symbols, say how many symbols each house gets, and say which house ran the most. Can the pictograph say how fast anyone ran?
items.final_answer: A key of 50 gives 3, 5, 2 and 4 symbols. Yamuna ran the most, 250 laps. The pictograph cannot say how fast anyone ran, because speed is not in its data

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: lists the numbers to be shown, each with its name
lays out each number in whole symbols and shows what is left over
adds every symbol the trial key would need
fixes a key that fits every number and draws the pictograph
ask the finished pictograph for the most, the least, the same and how many more
sets aside a question the data cannot answer, with those words across it
the chapter's three statements, ticked against work on the stage
turn over to show what data, tally marks, pictograph, symbol, title and key mean

teaching_notes: Give each group a data card before the tool is opened and let them try three keys, writing how many symbols each row would need, then draw the pictograph with the key they choose, and its title. Choosing a key is asked twice in the chapter, on the opening page and in the closing box, and taught nowhere. Take the route the chapter's own pictographs show: every key on its pages turns its data into whole symbols, or whole symbols and a half. So a key is checked against every number in turn, and a key that fits can still be too small to draw. Teach no other method. The opening page's airport data comes back here through the Concept Linking box: a key of one hundred flights gives fifteen, nine, six, five and four symbols. Call each airport by its city, and say the numbers are about, as the page does. The closing box's points take a key of fifty, giving four, five, six, seven, three and four symbols. Its three questions ask about the game itself, which the points cannot answer. Do not answer them; ask who scored the most, who the least and which two scored the same. The vocabulary box lists title and never defines it, and leaves out key. The title is the heading that says what a pictograph shows, and the key says what one symbol stands for.
generation_prompt: Build a key choosing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A data card at the left of the working area lists up to six named numbers, and a key dial beside it sets a trial key. A checker board to the right lays each number out as a row of one symbol at one size, one symbol per key's worth, from the same left edge. When nothing is left over the row lights; when exactly half the key is left over, a half symbol, the left half of the whole, closes the row and it lights; when anything else is left over, a loose tag at the row's end gives the number left over and the row stays unlit. A symbol count at the top left of the canvas adds every symbol the trial key needs, and a row too long for the board is drawn running off its edge. A set key control unlocks only when every row lights, and draws the pictograph with an outlined title strip and key box to fill. A stack of question cards asks the finished pictograph for the most, the least, the same and how many more; a card whose question the data cannot answer is set aside with the words not in this data. A can do list of three statements with tick boxes and six word cards that turn over run along the foot. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Pick a key. Check it on every number. Read what is left over. A half is fine. Count the symbols it needs. Draw the pictograph with a title and a key. Ask it what its data can answer.
